'''waistcoateer†''' (wāst-k tēr′), ''n.'' [Formerly ''wast-coateer'', ''wastcoati'' One who wears a wa garment, without a c the seventeenth and London, a prostitute ( dressed).
readings.c2s1:
{{smaller block|Who keeps the outward door there? here’s fine shuffling!
You ''waistcoateer'', you must go back.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, i. 1.}}
<poem>I knew you a ''waistcoateer'' in the garden alleys,

'''waistcoating''' (wāst′kọ̄t-ing, colloq. wes′kọ̄t-ing), ''n.'' A textile fabric made especially for men’s waistcoats, and different from cloth intended to be used for coats and trousers. These stuffs usually contain silk, and are of a fancy pattern.
{{smaller block|Mrs. Carver bespoke from him two pieces of ''waistcoating.'' {{right|''Miss Edgeworth'', The Dun, p. 315. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''waist-deep''' (wāst′dēp), ''a.'' and ''adv.'' So deep as to reach or be covered from the feet up to the waist: as, the ford was ''waist-deep.''
{{smaller block|<poem>The eager Knight leap’d in the sea
''Waist-deep'', and first on shore was he.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Lord of the Isles, v. 14.}}}}

'''waisted''' (wās′ted), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''wasted;'' < ''waist'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Having a waist (of some specified shape or type).
{{smaller block|<poem>''Med.'' I never saw a Coat better cut.
''Sir Fop.'' It makes me show long-''wasted.''</poem>
{{right|''Etherege'', Man of Mode, iii. 2.}}}}

'''waister''' (wās′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''waist'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A green hand on board a whaler, usually placed in the waist of the vessel until qualified for more responsible duties.—'''2.''' On a naval vessel, formerly, one of a class of old men who have been disabled or grown gray without rising in the service.

'''waist-high''' (wāst′hī), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''wast-high''; < ''waist'' + ''high''.] As high as the waist.
{{smaller block|Contemptible villages, . . . the grasse ''wast-high'', unmoved, uneaten.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 117.}}}}

'''waist-panel''' (wāst′pan″el), ''n.'' The panel immediately above the lowest panel on the outside of a carriage-body. ''Car-Builder’s Dict.'' [Eng.]

'''waist-piece''' (wāst′pēs), ''n.'' The steel skirt, or great braguette, of the armor of the fourteenth century. Compare cut under ''tasset.''

'''waist-rail''' (wāst′rāl), ''n.'' A horizontal piece in the framing of the side of a passenger-carriage. ''Car-Builder’s Dict.'' [Eng.]

'''waist-torque''' (wāst′tôrk), ''n.'' A girdle, properly one of twisted or spiral bars, worn by the northern nations in the early middle ages. Compare cut under ''torque.''

'''waist-tree''' (wāst′trē), ''n.'' A spare spar formerly placed along the waist of a ship where there were no bulwarks. Also called ''rough-tree.''

'''wait''' (wāt), ''n.'' [Formerly also, erroneously, ''waight''; < ME. ''waite'', ''wayte'', a watchman, spy, < OF. ''waite'', ''gaite'', a guard, sentinel, watchman, spy, later, ''guet'', watch, ward, heed, also the watch or company appointed to watch (= Pr. ''gach'', ''gayt''), < OHG. ''wahta'', MHG. ''wahte'', G. ''wacht'', a watchman; cf. Goth. ''wahtwo'', a watch, < AS. ''wacan'' = Goth. ''wakan'', etc., wake, watch: see ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, ''watch''. In senses 4, 5, 6, etc., the noun is from the verb.] '''1†.''' A watchman; a guard; also, a spy. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 513.
{{smaller block|<poem>And wysly bes ware [beware] ''waytys'' to the towne,
On yche half forto hede, that no harme fall.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 6265.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>And wysly bes ware [beware] ''waytys'' to the towne,

One of a body of musicians, especially in the seventeenth century in England. {{smaller|Originally the waits seem to have been watchmen who sounded horns, or in some other noisy way announced their being on watch. Bands of musicians seem to have borne the name generally at a later time, and it is still preserved in England, as applied to persons who sing out of doors at Christmas time, and seek gratuities from house to house.}}

{{smaller block|A ''wayte'', that nightelye from Mychelmas to Shreve Thorsdaye pipethe the watche withen this courte fower tymes. . . . Also this yeoman ''waight'', at the makinge of Knyghtes of the Bath, for his attendance upon them by nyghte-time, in watchinge in the chappelle, hath he to his fee all the watchinge clothing that the knyght shall wear upon him.
{{right|''Rymer'', quoted in Chambers’s Book of Days, II. 743.}}}}
{{smaller block|We will have the city ''waites'' down with us, and a noise of trumpets.
{{right|''Shirley'', Witty Fair One, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|There is scarce a young man of any fashion who does not make love with the town music. The ''waits'' often help him through his courtship; and my friend Banister has told me he was proffered five hundred pounds by a young fellow to play but one winter under the window of a lady.
{{right|''Tatler'', No. 222.}}}}
{{smaller block|A strain of music seemed to break forth in the air just below the window. I listened, and found it proceeded from a band, which I concluded to be the ''waits'' from some neighboring village.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 253.}}}}

'''3†.''' An old variety of hautboy or shawm: so called because much used by the waits.

<poem>Grete lordys were at the assent,
''Waytys'' blewe, to mete they wente.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''MS. Cantab.'' Ff. ii. 38, f. 69. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''waits'' or hoboys.
{{right|''Butler'', Principles of Musick (1636), quoted in [Chambers’s Book of Days, II. 743.}}}} '''4†.''' The act of watching; watchfulness.
{{smaller block|The nimbleness & ''wayt'' of the dog too take hiz auauntage, and the fors & experiens of the bear agayn to auoid the assauts.
{{right|''Robert Laneham'', Letter from Kenilworth (1575).}}}}
'''5†.''' An ambush; a trap; a plot: obsolete except in the phrase ''to lie in wait.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Fals semblance hath a visage ful demure,
Lightly to catche the ladies in a ''waite;''
Where-fore we must, if that we wil endure,
Make right good watche.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 78.}}}}
'''6.''' The act of waiting: as, a ''wait'' for the train at a station.—'''7.''' Time occupied in waiting; delay; an interval of waiting; specifically, in theatrical language, the time between two acts. Compare ''stage-wait.''
{{smaller block|It was thought I had suffered enough in my long ''wait'' for the trial.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', The Ladies Lindores, p. 98.}}}}
{{smaller block|During the ''wait'' between the first and second parts the Prince sent for Herr Schoenberger, a pianist who had pleased him very much, and personally complimented him.
{{right|''T. C. Crawford'', English Life, p. 141.}}}}
'''To lay wait.''' {{smaller|See ''lay''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''To lie in wait.''' {{smaller|See ''lie''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Waits’ badge,''' {{smaller|a badge formerly worn by town musicians, usually an escutcheon with the arms of the borough. Such badges exist in the treasuries of English towns and corporations.}}

'''wait''' (wāt), ''v.''   [< ME. ''waiten, wayten'', < OF. ''waiter, waitier, gaiter, gaitier, guetter'', F. ''guetter'' (Walloon ''weitier'') = Pr. ''gaitar, gachar'' = It. ''guatare'', watch, ward, mark, heed, note, lie in wait for, < OF. ''waite, gaite'', a guard, sentinel: see ''wait'', ''n''. Cf. ''await''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To watch; be on the watch; lie in wait; look out.
{{smaller block|He ''wayted'' after no pompe and reverence.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 525.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>William ful wiȝtly ''wayted'' out at an hole,
& seie breme burnes busi in ful briȝt armes.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2320.}}}}
'''2.''' To look forward to something; be in expectation: often with ''for''.
{{smaller block|She ''wayteth'' whan hir herte wolde breste.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 852.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Sil.'' And so, good rest.
''Pro.'' As wretches have o’er night
That ''wait for'' execution in the morn.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 2. 134.}}}}
{{smaller block|Both ''waited'' patiently, and yet both prayed for the accelerating of that which they ''waited for'': Daniel for the deliverance, Simeon for the Epiphany.
{{right|''Donne'', Sermons, iv.}}}}
'''3.''' To stay or rest in patience or expectation; remain in a state of quiescence or inaction, as till the arrival of some person or event, or till the proper moment or favorable opportunity for action: often with ''for''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bid them prepare within;
I am to blame to be thus ''waited for''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 2. 119.}}}}
{{smaller block|Do but ''wait'' till I despatch my tailor, and I’ll discover my device to you.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They also serve who only stand and ''wait.''
{{right|''Milton'', Sonnets, xiv.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The dinner ''waits'', and we are tir’d.
{{right|''Cowper'', John Gilpin.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|''Wait'' till we give you a dictionary, Sir! It takes Boston to do that thing, Sir!
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A tide of fierce
Invective seem’d to ''wait'' behind her lips,
As ''waits'' a river level with the dam,
Ready to burst and flood the world with foam.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}</poem>}}
'''4.''' To remain in readiness to execute orders; be ready to serve; be in waiting; perform the duties of an attendant or a servant; hence, to serve; supply the wants of persons at table.
{{smaller block|Thou [a page] art fitter to be worn in my cap than to ''wait'' at my heels. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|How one of the Serving-men, untrain’d to ''wait'', spilt the White-broth! {{right|''Brome'', Jovial Crew, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|Three large men, like doctors of divinity, ''wait'' behind the table, and furnish everything that appetite can ask for. {{right|''Thackeray'', Mrs. Perkins’s Ball.}}}}

'''To wait on''' or '''upon'''.   [''On'', prep.]   (''a''†) To watch; guard.
{{smaller block|Loke that ye ''waite'' well ''vpon'' me, and yef it be myster cometh me to helpe. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 647.}}}}
(''b''†) To look at; look toward.
{{smaller block|The eyes of all ''wait upon'' thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. {{right|Ps. cxlv. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is a point of cunning to ''wait upon'' him with whom you speak, with your eye. {{right|''Bacon'', Cunning (ed. 1887).}}}}
(''c''†) To lie in wait for.
{{smaller block|<poem>This somnour evere ''waitynge on'' his prey.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Friar’s Tale, l. 76.}}</poem>}}
(''d''†) To expect; look for.
{{smaller block|<poem>I wot the in witte to ''waite on'' myn end.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7943.}}</poem>}} (e†) To attend to; perform, as a duty.

{{smaller block|According to the grace that is given unto us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy, . . . or ministry, let us ''wait on'' our ministering.
{{right|Rom. xii. 7.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
